parts.name: Arrival
parts.stand: Outside the museum entrance, before you go in.

paras.t: This is the Regional Museum of Messina. It tells the story of art in this city from the 1100s to the 1700s, and much of it was pulled from the ruins of the 1908 earthquake.

The museum itself is a survivor. It first opened in 1806, to end, as the phrase went, the despoliation of art. In 1908 the building collapsed in the earthquake, and some works were lost. The major pieces were brought indoors; the rest waited in makeshift shelters and out on the open esplanade.

Then came the long wait for a proper home. Until 2017 the collection lived in a former silk mill. Building work began in 1984, and the museum only opened fully on June 17, 2017. Along the way, in 1951, someone discovered that paintings had been stolen and replaced with fakes.
It's a big place. Take your time, and sit down whenever a painting asks you to.

parts.name: The old city in pieces
parts.stand: In the medieval galleries; ask the staff if you can't find them.

paras.t: A lot of what's here is old Messina in pieces: paintings, sculpture and decoration from buildings the earthquake damaged or destroyed.
Look for the painted wooden beams from the cathedral ceiling, from the 1200s and 1300s. Their scenes include warrior angels, Saint George, and Jonah coming out of the whale's mouth.

And look for the colored marble inlay panels, gathered here from the city's churches after 1908. Centuries earlier, Messina was probably the first Sicilian city to host Byzantine artisans skilled in this kind of inlay.

Before we get to Antonello, a word of warning. Wikipedia reports that on August 15, 2026, three panels of Antonello da Messina's San Gregorio Polyptych, and another panel attributed to him, were stolen from this museum overnight. We don't know whether they've come back, so ask the staff what's on display today.
The museum's director at the time, Marisa Mercurio, called it a great loss for the museum, for the city, the community and the art world.

parts.name: Antonello da Messina
parts.stand: In the Antonello room; ask the staff if you can't find it.

paras.t: Antonello da Messina is this city's own painter of the early Renaissance, born here around 1429 to 1431. His San Gregorio Polyptych, from 1473, is the Antonello this museum is known for, though some of its panels were reported stolen in 2026, so you may find gaps.

His work shows a strong influence from Netherlandish painting, though there's no record that he ever traveled beyond Italy. The old biographer Vasari even credited him with bringing oil painting to Italy, but historians now regard that as wrong.
He was also a pioneer of the portrait. The art historian John Pope-Hennessy called him the first Italian painter for whom the individual portrait was an art form in its own right.
He spent 1475 and 1476 in Venice, and his work influenced painters there. Then he came home, and he died here in Messina in 1479. His son Jacobello finished some of his last works.

parts.name: Neptune and Scylla
parts.stand: At Montorsoli's Scylla; ask the staff where it's shown.

paras.t: This Scylla is by Montorsoli, the sculptor of the fountains by the cathedral and on Via Garibaldi. The museum also lists the original of his Neptune fountain, so look for that too.

Scylla belongs to the strait outside. In Greek myth she's a man-eating monster living on one side of a narrow channel, opposite the sea-swallowing monster Charybdis. Virgil, in the Aeneid, linked that channel with the Strait of Messina.

In the myth as Homer's Odyssey tells it, Odysseus gets through the strait, but Scylla snatches six of his sailors off the deck. Out on Via Garibaldi, the fountain still shows Neptune with Scylla and Charybdis.
Here are two paintings by Caravaggio from his time in Sicily: the Raising of Lazarus and the Adoration of the Shepherds.
He came here a man on the run. In Rome he had killed Ranuccio Tomassoni in a brawl and been sentenced to death. He fled to Naples, then Malta, then Sicily, hoping for a pardon from the pope.

With his old friend Mario Minniti, he made what amounted to a triumphal tour from Syracuse to Messina, winning prestigious, well-paid commissions. Look at how he paints: his great Sicilian altarpieces isolate their shadowy, pitifully poor figures in vast areas of darkness.
In the Lazarus, look at the body. It's still stiff with death, but the hand, turned toward Christ's, is alive.

He wasn't easy company. Reports from the time describe him sleeping fully armed and in his clothes, ripping up a painting at a slight word of criticism, and mocking local painters. After only nine months in Sicily he went back to Naples, in the late summer of 1609. He died the next year, and how he died is still uncertain.
Keep an eye out for two paintings that echo the cathedral square: Mattia Preti's Madonna of the Letter, and a painting called Orion, Founder of Messina.
So much in this building was dug out of rubble, sheltered, moved and, more than once, stolen. What's on these walls is here because people kept digging it out and putting it back.
